claim.text: Two successive strengthenings of the ordinary non-desklamp exact-target rule show the same adherence limit: the rule has not reliably prevented a Candidate from manipulating a near-match object when the exact target is absent, and has not converted such an absent-target failure into success. The S1_R05-era edit required that, when the exact noun phrase had not been observed, the Actor not acquire, clean, cool, heat or place a different but related object; in that round's clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer pair the exact butterknife was absent, drawer 1 held knife 1 and spatula 1, and the Candidate took the near-miss knife, cleaned it and moved it (v23_4_R05_replay_v3_validation_001/P7:2, .../Q7:4, .../P7:8, .../Q7:9, .../Q7:17, .../Q7:19) while both sides reached the 50-step limit. The current diff instead requires confirming an object's exact category name before acquiring, cleaning, cooling, heating or placing it and explicitly names near-matches to reject (knife vs butterknife, soapbottle vs soapbar, cup vs mug, spraybottle vs soapbottle); in the same task this round, drawer 1 again held knife 1 and spatula 1 (P7:2, Q7:4), no butterknife was found in the observed search, and the Candidate again took the near-match knife (Q7:9), cleaned it (Q7:17) and placed it in drawer 1 (Q7:19), as did the Parent (P7:5, P7:7, P7:9); both hit the 50-step limit. In the R05 put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair the exact soapbar was also absent and neither side picked up a near-miss, yet both also hit the limit. So the stricter wording neither reliably suppressed near-match manipulation nor produced success where the exact target was not located.
